title: Value is desirability plus scarcity, and it is being reshuffled
description: A strategist's half-hour on what value actually is: something people want that is hard to get elsewhere, not the product itself and not a solved problem. He sorts value into relief (fix, protect, save) and desire (identity, pleasure, belonging, meaning), warns against five kinds of fake value (a different process, the category's generic value, a bolted-on USP, a company's values, words and positioning alone), and gives three games for finding new value: importing another category's value, selling the category to people outside it, and cultivating a weakness competitors cannot copy. For Maia City it is a test for every COOP and offer: what do people get from it, is it scarce, is it new, and is the whole organisation built to make that one thing.
summary: **Value is what people get, measured against how easy it is to get elsewhere.** Desirability alone is utility; without scarcity it earns nothing, as water and gold show. Value can be material or emotional and is as real either way: what a jeweller's name adds to a diamond is value even though it cannot be weighed. Problem solving is one legitimate way to create it, not the purpose of business, and many large businesses solve no apparent problem.

**Two families of value, and five kinds of fake value.** Relief gives people what they need: fixing, protecting against a risk, saving time, money or effort. Desire gives them what they want: identity, pleasure, belonging, meaning and growth. Fake value is a different process with the same output, the generic value every competitor in the category already delivers, an isolated unique selling point, a company's purpose that customers get nothing from, and messaging or positioning that changes words but not what the world gets.

**Value is being reshuffled, so look for what is new and build everything around it.** What was scarce or desirable is changing fast, so the old rules of thumb fail and value has to be rethought from first principles; "new" is a harder standard than "unique", and finding it is innovation. Three games help: mix in the generic value of an unrelated category, sell the category's abstract value to people who do not shop it yet through a channel others ignore, and cultivate a weakness that unlocks value competitors cannot follow. Then the strategy hierarchy holds: the value at the top, the product that makes it below, the brand that carries it below that.
